courses.title: CARSI Water Restoration Practitioner
courses.description:
A foundational, Australian-produced course for restoration technicians, supervisors, cleaners and insurance-support staff who respond to water-damaged buildings and contents. It builds sound field judgement — it does not replace a technician’s own certification, a manufacturer’s instructions, a Safety Data Sheet, or a site’s own rules.

Six modules take a new technician from first principles to a defensible job file: what water damage restoration is and how to think about it, how water is categorised (Category 1/2/3) and classified by the extent of intrusion, hazard-led safety and PPE selection, moisture assessment with metric instruments and Australian-available equipment, drying principles with realistic 230 V / 10 A power awareness, and documentation, reporting and the Australian insurance context. Each idea is grounded in Australian power (230 V, 50 Hz, 10 A GPO, RCD/safety switch), metric units, Australian standards and regulators (AS/NZS, Safe Work Australia, state WHS regulators), and Australian job realities. Each module ends with a check, and a final knowledge check closes the course.

CARSI Water Restoration Practitioner is a CARSI Southern Hemisphere Restoration Designation. Standards are referenced by name only (for example, aligned to the principles in ANSI/IICRC S500); no standard text is reproduced.

modules.title: Module 1: Course Objectives & How This Training Works

lessons.title: What this course covers and who it is for
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Scenario and figures are illustrative and flagged for verification.

On the job

A property manager in Brisbane rings on a Monday morning. A ground-floor unit lost a flexible hose under the kitchen sink some time over the weekend, and the tenant has just reported it. Water has tracked from the kitchen along a timber-look floor into the hallway and under the skirting. The manager wants to know what will happen, how long it will take and what it will cost. Your first job is not to start drying — it is to size the loss, make it safe and set expectations.

The idea

Welcome to the CARSI Water Restoration Practitioner course. It is written for technicians, supervisors, cleaners and insurance-support staff who attend water-damaged buildings and contents in Australia. By the end you will be able to describe what professional water damage restoration is and why a structured process matters; categorise water by likely contamination (Category 1, 2 and 3) and describe how the extent of intrusion is classified; identify site hazards and select personal protective equipment (PPE) by the hazard in front of you rather than by habit; take and interpret moisture readings with metric instruments and set a defensible dry goal; explain the principles of structural drying and size equipment with realistic power awareness at 230 V / 10 A; and produce documentation that stands up in an Australian insurance and dispute context.

The course is built for Australian conditions throughout. That means Australian English, 230 V / 50 Hz power delivered through 10 A general power outlets (GPOs) protected by a residual current device (RCD, or safety switch), metric measurement, Australian standards and regulators (AS/NZS, Safe Work Australia and your state work-health-and-safety regulator), and Australian building types, climate and job realities. It supports good judgement. It does not replace your own certification, a manufacturer’s instructions, a Safety Data Sheet (SDS), a relevant Australian standard, or a site’s own rules. Where a standard is named, it is named only (for example, aligned to the principles in ANSI/IICRC S500); its text is never reproduced.

See it

The roadmap shows how the six modules build on one another, from first principles to a complete, defensible job file.

Do it in metric

Size the Brisbane loss before you quote anything. The kitchen is 4.2 m × 3.0 m = 12.6 m². Water has also tracked into a hallway 3.5 m × 1.0 m = 3.5 m². The affected floor area is therefore about 12.6 + 3.5 = 16.1 m². You record the ambient air on arrival at 24 °C and 70 %RH. These two numbers — affected area in m² and the starting air condition — are the first entries in the job file and the basis of every later decision.

Field download

The First-attendance roadmap card lists the order of the first hour on site: make safe, size the loss in m², record the air condition, identify the water, and set expectations with the customer. Keep it in the van.

Check yourself

The module check asks: what is the first task on arrival; which metric figure sizes the loss; and why you record the starting air condition. Each answer carries a short practitioner “why”.

Takeaway

Restoration starts with sizing and safety, not with machines. Record the affected area in m² and the air condition at the first attendance. Next lesson: how the restoration mindset turns these first numbers into a repeatable process.

lessons.title: How the restoration mindset works
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Timings and figures are illustrative and flagged for verification.

On the job

A technician in Geelong arrives at a rented house where a washing-machine hose failed on Friday night and ran until Sunday. The floor looks almost dry on top, so the owner assumes the job is small. The technician knows better: two days of water in a cool, closed house means the skirting, the wall base and the underlay are likely still wet, and the clock on microbial growth has been running the whole time. The mindset, not the surface, drives the plan.

The idea

Water damage restoration is a race between drying and damage. Wet materials do not just look bad — over hours and days they support microbial growth, corrosion, swelling and delamination. The professional aim is to return the structure and the restorable contents to a dry, safe condition quickly, safely and with evidence, and to know when a material should be restored rather than removed.

A reliable job follows a repeatable arc, whatever the size of the loss: make it safe; understand the water and the affected materials; control the source and remove bulk water; assess moisture and set a dry goal; apply the right drying strategy; monitor to the goal; then verify and document. Each step feeds the next, and skipping one almost always shows up later as a callback or a disputed claim. Australia adds its own constraints at every step — 230 V power on 10 A circuits, metric measurement, Australian climate and building types, and Australian work-health-and-safety law — so the arc is the same everywhere but the detail is local. Where a standard is referenced it is named nominatively (for example, aligned to the principles in ANSI/IICRC S500) and never reproduced. The mindset also means honesty about limits: if a hazard cannot be controlled, or a material is beyond restoration, the professional decision is to stop, remove or escalate rather than press on.

See it

The arc reads left to right; monitoring loops back until the dry goal is reached.

Do it in metric

Put a number on why speed matters. A failed washing-machine hose can discharge roughly 2 L/min. Running from Friday 9 pm to Sunday 9 am is 36 hours, or 2160 minutes. At 2 L/min that is about 2 × 2160 = 4320 L — more than 4000 litres through the house. Even if most drained away, the materials left holding water at 22 °C have had 36 hours to wick and to support growth. The volume explains the urgency.

Field download

The First-attendance roadmap card also carries the restoration arc on its reverse, so the order of work is in your hand on every job.

Check yourself

The module check asks you to put the steps of the arc in order, explain why surface dryness is misleading, and estimate a discharge volume. Each answer carries a practitioner “why”.

Takeaway

Follow the arc every time: safe, understand, control, assess, dry, monitor, verify, document. Surface dryness is not proof. Next lesson (Module 2): how water is categorised by contamination.

lessons.title: The three water categories
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Scenario and figures are illustrative and flagged for verification.

On the job

In a Perth townhouse a toilet has overflowed into the adjoining hallway. The owner has already mopped the visible water and says it is “just water”. You need to decide, before anyone touches it again, whether this is clean, grey or black water — because that one call drives the PPE, the cleaning, what can be saved and how the waste is handled. Getting it wrong either exposes people to contamination or writes off materials that could have been kept.

The idea

Water is described by how contaminated it is likely to be. Three categories are used. Category 1 — clean water originates from a sanitary source with no substantial contamination, for example a burst mains supply line, an overflowing tap, or rainwater that has not passed through contaminated materials. Category 2 — significantly contaminated (“grey water”) contains contamination that could cause discomfort or illness if contacted or consumed, for example discharge from a dishwasher or washing machine, or a toilet overflow containing urine but no faeces. Category 3 — grossly contaminated (“black water”) may contain harmful agents, for example sewage, water from beyond the toilet trap, or floodwater from rivers or the sea.

Two rules matter on site. First, a category can worsen over time: clean water left in a warm, closed building can degrade toward Category 2 or 3 as it contacts soils and supports growth, so a Monday reassessment of a Friday loss may land in a worse category than the first visit. Second, when you are unsure, treat the water as the worse category and reassess rather than guess optimistically. The category is a practitioner judgement recorded in the job file with the reasons behind it — the source, the materials contacted, the time elapsed and the building conditions — because it drives every safety, PPE, cleaning and disposal decision that follows. A vulnerable occupant (very young, elderly or immune-compromised) raises the bar further.

See it

The diagram pairs each category with typical Australian sources and the way clean water can degrade.

Do it in metric

Quantify the Perth overflow before you decide. The pan holds and releases roughly 6 L per flush; the cistern adds about 9 L, so a stuck flush can put 15 L across the floor in under a minute. The water is urine-contaminated but shows no faeces, and it has sat for about 3 hours at 27 °C. That evidence — source, visible contamination, 15 L spread and 3 hours at 27 °C — supports a Category 2 call, recorded with its reasons, and a watch for degradation.

Field download

The Water category and class decision card walks the source, the contamination seen, the time and the building conditions to a defensible category, with a prompt to reassess.

Check yourself

The module check asks you to place sources into categories, explain why a category can worsen, and justify a borderline call. Each answer carries a practitioner “why”.

Takeaway

Category is about contamination, not amount. When unsure, treat as the worse category and reassess. Record the reasons. Next lesson: classes — how much water and how hard it will be to dry.

lessons.title: Classes: how much water and how hard to dry
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Figures are illustrative and flagged for verification.

On the job

Two jobs land on the same day. One is a small laundry in Adelaide where a tap fitting wept overnight onto a vinyl floor. The other is a Cairns unit where a roof leak in a storm soaked the ceiling, the wall insulation and the carpet in the main bedroom. Both are “water damage”, but they need very different amounts of drying capacity. The difference is the class, and reading it correctly is how you size the job and avoid both under-drying and over-resourcing.

The idea

Where category describes contamination, class describes the amount of water and the likely rate of evaporation — in plain terms, how big the drying job is. In broad terms: Class 1 is the least water, with only part of a room or low-porosity materials affected, and it dries fastest. Class 2 is a larger amount — an entire room, carpet and underlay, and wicking up walls to roughly 300 mm. Class 3 is the greatest amount, with ceilings, walls, insulation and subfloor saturated, often because the water came from above. Class 4 is specialty drying: water bound in low-permeability materials such as hardwood, plaster, masonry or concrete that dry very slowly and need specialist methods and patience.

Class shapes how much airflow and dehumidification you need and how long the job will take. The Adelaide laundry is a small, low-class job; the Cairns bedroom, wet from above with saturated insulation, is a high-class job needing far more equipment and a containment strategy. Getting the class right early prevents under-drying — which returns as a callback and a possible mould claim — and prevents over-resourcing, which wastes equipment and power you may not have on a 10 A circuit. Class is recorded alongside category in the job file, and both are revisited as materials are opened up and the true extent is seen. In the humid tropics the same class of loss is harder to dry than in a dry inland winter, so the class sets the scale and the local climate sets the effort.

See it

The diagram shows the wetted footprint growing from Class 1 to Class 3 and the bound-water case of Class 4.

Do it in metric

Estimate the wetted area in the Cairns bedroom. The room is 5.0 m × 4.0 m, so the floor is 20 m². The walls are wet from the ceiling down, and the perimeter is (5.0 + 4.0) × 2 = 18 m. With the full wall height wet rather than only wicking to 300 mm, this is clearly a Class 3 loss. Compare the Adelaide laundry: wicking only to 300 mm over a 6 m perimeter is 6 × 0.3 = 1.8 m² of wall — a small Class 1 to 2 job.

Field download

The Water category and class decision card includes a class ready-reckoner: wetted footprint, wall-wicking height in mm and whether water came from above.

Check yourself

The module check asks you to match losses to classes, explain the callback risk of a wrong class, and read a wall-wicking height. Each answer carries a practitioner “why”.

Takeaway

Category is contamination; class is quantity and difficulty. Read the class to size the drying and the power. Next (Module 3): making the job safe and choosing PPE by the hazard.

lessons.title: Identify the hazards first
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Scenario and figures are illustrative and flagged for verification.

On the job

You arrive at a Melbourne home where a hot-water system burst in a garage-turned-rumpus room. There is standing water across the floor and a power board with leads running to a bar fridge and a television sits just above it. The temptation is to wade in and start extracting. The right first move is to stop at the threshold, look for what can hurt someone, and control it — because water and 230 V mains are a fatal combination and no carpet is worth a life.

The idea

Safety comes before drying. Under the model Work Health and Safety (WHS) laws administered through Safe Work Australia and adopted by your state regulator, the person conducting the business or undertaking (PCBU) must eliminate risks so far as is reasonably practicable, and if that is not possible, minimise them — working down the hierarchy of controls, where elimination is strongest and PPE is the last line. Hazards are identified and controlled before work begins, usually recorded in a Safe Work Method Statement (SWMS) or job safety analysis, with a site induction where one is required.

Common water-damage hazards include: electrical — water and 230 V mains do not mix, so do not enter standing water near live fittings, have the supply isolated where needed, and run portable equipment through a residual current device (safety switch, RCD); all portable electrical gear should be inspected, tested and tagged by a competent person in line with AS/NZS 3760. Biological — Category 2 and 3 water carries micro-organisms, and sewage is a biohazard. Slips, trips and falls — wet floors, trailing leads and ladders. Structural — saturated ceilings and floors can collapse, and a wet plaster ceiling holding water is a serious overhead hazard. Chemical — cleaning and antimicrobial products; always read the SDS. Confined spaces and heat — subfloors, roof voids and hot drying environments. If a hazard cannot be controlled, the correct decision may be to stop and escalate — to a licensed electrician or a structural engineer, or to the Poisons Information Centre on 13 11 26 for a chemical exposure, or 000 in an emergency.

See it

The map walks a flooded room and marks where each hazard type typically hides.

Do it in metric

Make the Melbourne room electrically safe before anything else. The standing water sits around a power board fed from a 230 V, 10 A GPO. You do not reach for the leads — you isolate the circuit at the switchboard, confirm it is dead, and only then connect your own extraction gear through a portable RCD that disconnects on a small earth-leakage fault (an RCD is designed to trip at a leakage of about 30 mA). Every lead you plug in is current-tagged under AS/NZS 3760.

Field download

The Hazard-to-PPE selection card opens with a hazard walk-through: electrical, biological, structural, chemical, slip and heat, each with its first control.

Check yourself

The module check asks which hazard is controlled first, who holds the primary duty, and when to stop and escalate. Each answer carries a practitioner “why”.

Takeaway

Identify and control hazards before drying; elimination beats PPE. Isolate power, use an RCD, work with tested-and-tagged leads. Next lesson: choosing PPE by the hazard present.

lessons.title: Select PPE by the hazard present
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Figures are illustrative and flagged for verification.

On the job

A sewage backflow has pushed black water into a Darwin ground-floor flat. One technician reaches for the same gloves and dust mask they wear on a clean-water job. The supervisor stops them: this is Category 3 work, and the PPE that was fine this morning on a burst mains line is not enough here. The hazard in front of you — not the job you did last — sets what you wear, and the choice is written into the job file.

The idea

PPE is chosen for the hazard in front of you, then recorded in the job file. It is the last line of defence, after isolation and engineering controls have done their work. A practical guide by category and task: for Category 1 (clean water), safety footwear, gloves and eye protection, plus respiratory protection if you will disturb dusty or already-mouldy materials. For Category 2 (grey water), the above plus fluid-resistant gloves and a correctly fitted P2 respirator when generating aerosols or handling contaminated materials. For Category 3 (black water / sewage), full skin protection — fluid-resistant coveralls, gloves, boots and eye protection — with P2 (or higher) respiratory protection fit-checked to the wearer, and everything contacted treated as contaminated.

Respirators only protect when they seal. A tight-fitting respirator needs the right size and a clean-shaven seal; facial hair under the seal breaks it, in which case a loose-fitting powered respirator is used instead. Record the PPE actually used, not just the PPE available, because the job file has to show the control that was in place at the time. Where mould is present, respiratory and skin protection are selected for the mould hazard as well — that is covered in CARSI’s separate mould remediation course, which this course links to rather than repeats. The same discipline applies to gloves and eye protection: match the chemical to its SDS, and change damaged or contaminated PPE rather than pushing on. PPE is never a substitute for isolating power or removing grossly contaminated material — it backs up those higher controls, it does not replace them.

See it

The diagram stacks the PPE set as the category rises from 1 to 3.

Do it in metric

Set the threshold for respiratory protection. On the Darwin job you will be hosing and extracting, which generates aerosols, and you will disturb more than 1 m² of sewage-contaminated material. That triggers at least a fit-checked P2 respirator, fluid-resistant coveralls and boots. You confirm the seal on each wearer before entry — a respirator that leaks at the face gives close to 0 % of its rated protection, so an unfit-tested mask is treated as no protection at all.

Field download

The Hazard-to-PPE selection card sets out the PPE set for each category and the fit-check prompt, so the right gear is chosen before entry.

Check yourself

The module check asks you to match PPE to category, explain why fit matters, and record PPE correctly. Each answer carries a practitioner “why”.

Takeaway

Choose PPE for the hazard present, confirm the seal, and record what was worn. Category 3 means full skin and respiratory protection. Next (Module 4): measuring moisture.

lessons.title: Instruments and what they tell you
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Instrument brands and figures are illustrative and flagged for verification (availability check 2026-07-09).

On the job

A Sydney apartment had a slow shower-recess leak. The tiles look fine and the owner cannot see a problem, but there is a musty note in the hallway cupboard that backs onto the wet wall. Without instruments you are guessing. With them, you can show exactly where the moisture is, how wet the materials are, and whether the air is helping or hindering drying — and you can prove all of it with numbers in the job file.

The idea

You cannot dry what you cannot measure. Moisture assessment uses several instruments, each answering a different question, and all read in metric. Non-invasive (capacitance or radio-frequency) meters scan a surface without leaving pinholes, so you can map where moisture is, quickly. Pin (resistance) moisture meters give a quantitative reading in a specific material such as timber or plaster, usually as a percentage or a wood-moisture-equivalent scale. Thermo-hygrometers read air temperature in °C and relative humidity in %RH, from which you work out dew point and specific humidity — the grams of water carried per kilogram of dry air (g/kg), which is the number that tells you whether the air can still accept moisture. Thermal imaging cameras show temperature patterns that suggest where evaporative cooling, and therefore moisture, may be; a thermal indication is always confirmed with a moisture meter before you act on it.

Instruments sold in Australia in 230 V or battery form — brands such as Protimeter, Tramex, Delmhorst and FLIR are widely distributed here — are the practical toolkit (availability last checked 2026-07-09; the SME should confirm current models). Calibrate and check instruments against the manufacturer’s instructions, because an uncalibrated meter produces confident but wrong numbers, and confident wrong numbers in a job file are worse than none. Record the instrument used and its mode beside each reading, so another technician can repeat the measurement the same way on the next visit. The instrument does not make the decision — you do — but it gives the decision an evidence base.

See it

The diagram pairs each instrument with the question it answers and its metric output.

Do it in metric

Read the air in the Sydney hallway. The thermo-hygrometer shows 24 °C and 70 %RH. At that condition the air carries roughly 13 g/kg of water, and the dew point is about 18 °C. The same meter in an unaffected room reads 24 °C and 55 %RH, about 10 g/kg. The 3 g/kg difference between the affected and unaffected air confirms there is extra moisture being released into the hallway — evidence to open up the cupboard wall and meter the material directly.

Field download

The Moisture map and dry-goal sheet has a column for the instrument and mode beside every reading, so the method is recorded, not just the number.

Check yourself

The module check asks which instrument answers which question, why a thermal hit is confirmed with a meter, and what g/kg tells you. Each answer carries a practitioner “why”.

Takeaway

Each instrument answers one question; record the instrument and read everything in metric. Confirm thermal hits with a meter. Next lesson: mapping moisture and setting the dry goal.

lessons.title: Mapping moisture and setting a dry goal
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Figures are illustrative and flagged for verification.

On the job

A Hobart cottage took water across the lounge from a failed heater valve. You have found the wet area, but the owner and the insurer will both ask the same question in a week: is it dry yet? If your only answer is “it feels dry”, you have nothing. If you set a dry goal on day one and track every point back to it, you can prove the job is finished the day the numbers say so — and defend it months later if the claim is questioned.

The idea

A defensible drying job starts with a dry standard — a reference reading taken from the same material in an unaffected area of the same building, with the same instrument and mode. That reference is your target: you dry the wet material back to the reference reading, not to an arbitrary number pulled from memory. Timber in a Hobart cottage sits at a different equilibrium from timber in a Darwin flat, so the reference is always local to the building and the season.

Map the affected area on day one. Mark the boundary of the moisture, record readings at labelled points on a sketch, note the material and the instrument at each point, and photograph the readings. Repeat at the same labelled points on each visit so the numbers are directly comparable and show a trend. A drying job is complete when the affected materials reach the dry standard and the readings are stable on the next visit — measured, not assumed. Keep everything metric: metres and millimetres for extent, °C and %RH for air, and grams per kilogram for specific humidity. This measured trail is what later proves the structure was returned to a dry, safe condition, and it is the difference between a professional file and a story. If a reading will not fall, the map tells you where to look — an unopened cavity, a bound material, or equipment that is undersized or switched off — rather than leaving you guessing across the whole room.

See it

The sketch shows numbered points, the wet boundary and the dry-reference point used to set the goal.

Do it in metric

Set a goal for the Hobart lounge. Unaffected skirting of the same timber reads 12 % on the pin meter — that is your dry standard. Wet skirting by the valve reads 28 %. You record readings at points spaced about every 1 m along the wet wall (a 4 m wall gives four points) and log the air at 21 °C and 60 %RH. The dry goal for every wet timber point is 12 %, stable on the following visit, across the roughly 15 m² affected floor.

Field download

The Moisture map and dry-goal sheet provides the room sketch, the numbered-point table, the dry-reference line and a per-visit trend column.

Check yourself

The module check asks what a dry standard is, why you read the same points each visit, and when drying is complete. Each answer carries a practitioner “why”.

Takeaway

Set the dry goal from an unaffected reference, map numbered points, and dry to the goal, not to a feeling. Next (Module 5): the drying principles that get you there.

lessons.title: The drying equation: heat, airflow and humidity
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Psychrometric figures are illustrative and flagged for verification.

On the job

In a humid Gold Coast summer a technician sets six air movers blasting across a wet Class 2 lounge and goes home pleased. Two days later the carpet is no drier, the windows are streaming and the room smells worse. Airflow alone did not dry the room — it just lifted moisture into air that had nowhere to put it. Drying is not about blowing air; it is about managing water in air, and that is a balance you can reason about.

The idea

Structural drying is applied psychrometrics — the behaviour of water in air. Four levers control the rate of drying. Evaporation: moving air across a wet surface speeds evaporation, which is what air movers do. Dehumidification: removing the evaporated moisture from the air so drying can continue, using refrigerant or desiccant dehumidifiers. Temperature: warmer air holds and releases moisture more readily, within sensible limits. Air exchange or containment: either bringing in drier outside air, or sealing the area so your equipment controls the environment rather than fighting the whole building.

The balance is the whole point. Adding airflow without dehumidification simply raises the humidity in the room and stalls drying, and in a closed, humid space it risks secondary damage such as condensation and mould. You add evaporative energy and remove moisture together, then measure the result in g/kg to confirm the air inside the drying zone is drier than the air outside it. Relative humidity on its own can mislead because it moves with temperature; specific humidity (g/kg) is the honest measure of how much water the air is actually carrying, which is why professionals track it. Australian climate shapes the strategy: a humid coastal summer on the Gold Coast or in Cairns needs far more dehumidification and often containment, while a dry inland winter may let controlled ventilation do much of the work. The levers are the same across the country; the mix changes with the weather outside the door, and the only way to know the mix is working is to measure it.

See it

The diagram balances moisture released by evaporation against moisture removed by dehumidification and exchange.

Do it in metric

Show why the dehumidifier matters. On the Gold Coast the room air starts at 30 °C and 60 %RH, carrying roughly 16 g/kg. A refrigerant dehumidifier conditions the air to about 24 °C and 45 %RH, roughly 8.4 g/kg. That is about 16 − 8.4 = 7.6 g/kg of water pulled out of each kilogram of air — capacity the air movers can then use to pick up more moisture from the carpet. Without the dehumidifier, the same air movers only recirculate 16 g/kg air and nothing dries.

Field download

The Drying and power-budget worksheet includes a psychrometry quick-check: record inside and outside g/kg each visit and confirm inside is lower.

Check yourself

The module check asks you to name the four levers, explain why airflow alone stalls, and read a g/kg drop. Each answer carries a practitioner “why”.

Takeaway

Evaporate and dehumidify together, and prove it in g/kg. Airflow without moisture removal makes things worse. Next lesson: the equipment, the power budget and the mould rule.

lessons.title: Equipment, power budgeting and the mould rule
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Equipment current draws are illustrative; the SME should confirm against rating plates (availability check 2026-07-09).

On the job

A technician in a Newcastle unit plugs a dehumidifier and four air movers into the two GPOs in the lounge, both on the same kitchen circuit, and heads off for the night. At 2 am the breaker trips. The drying stops, unnoticed, for seven hours, and the next morning the readings have barely moved. The equipment was fine; the power plan was not. On 230 V / 10 A circuits, power is a constraint you budget for, not an afterthought.

The idea

The core drying kit is air movers (to drive evaporation), dehumidifiers (to remove moisture), air filtration devices / air scrubbers (to manage airborne particulates), and heat where appropriate. In Australia this equipment runs on 230 V, 50 Hz and plugs into 10 A GPOs, so the power available is a real limit on how many machines you can run in one place.

Budget the power before you deploy. A single 10 A circuit delivers roughly 230 V × 10 A = 2300 W in total, and several outlets in a room often share one circuit breaker back at the board. Add up each machine’s actual current draw from its rating plate, in amps at 230 V, and keep the total on any one circuit safely below its rating, allowing headroom for motor start-up surges. A low-grain-refrigerant (LGR) dehumidifier plus a few air movers can approach a single circuit’s limit on its own. Overloading either trips the breaker — so drying stops silently overnight — or, worse, overheats wiring. Spread the load across separate circuits, run through an RCD, and use only inspected, tested-and-tagged leads.

There is one hard rule that changes the sequence: mould. If visible mould is present, do not run air movers — high airflow across mouldy surfaces aerosolises spores and spreads contamination through the building. While mould is present, dry using air filtration devices and dehumidifiers only, under containment, and bring air movers in only after remediation and a clearance confirm the mould has been dealt with. When in doubt, treat suspected mould as mould and hold the air movers. Mould remediation itself is a separate CARSI course.

See it

The diagram adds machine current draws against the 2300 W limit of one 10 A circuit and splits the load.

Do it in metric

Budget the Newcastle lounge properly. An LGR dehumidifier draws 4.5 A and each air mover draws 1.2 A. One dehumidifier plus four air movers is 4.5 + (4 × 1.2) = 4.5 + 4.8 = 9.3 A — above a safe working load for a single 10 A circuit once start-up surges are added. The fix is to split the load: put the dehumidifier and two air movers (4.5 + 2.4 = 6.9 A) on one circuit and the other two air movers (2.4 A) on a separate circuit.

Field download

The Drying and power-budget worksheet totals machine amps per circuit against the 10 A limit and flags the mould hold-rule before any air mover is placed.

Check yourself

The module check asks you to total a circuit load, explain the silent-overnight-trip risk, and apply the mould rule. Each answer carries a practitioner “why”.

Takeaway

Budget amps per 10 A circuit and split the load; a tripped breaker dries nothing. If mould is present, hold the air movers. Next (Module 6): documentation and the insurance context.

modules.title: Module 6: Documentation, Reporting & the Australian Insurance Context

lessons.title: Build a defensible job file
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Figures are illustrative and flagged for verification.

On the job

Four months after a Canberra drying job, the insurer’s assessor rings: the owner says a bedroom still smells and is blaming the restoration. The technician who did the work has left. Everything now rests on the job file. If it holds dated photos, a moisture map, daily readings trending to a dry goal and a record of what was removed and why, the business is protected. If it holds a one-line invoice, it is one person’s word against another’s.

The idea

If it is not documented, it did not happen. A professional water-damage job file records, from the first attendance: the loss — cause, category and class, and the date and time of attendance; photographs of the affected areas, the source and the damage; a moisture map with labelled readings, the dry standard, the instruments used, and repeat readings each visit; the drying plan — the equipment placed, where, and why, including the power arrangements; daily monitoring — air temperature, %RH, specific humidity in g/kg and material readings, trending toward the dry goal; safety — hazards identified, controls applied, PPE used, and any specialist called; and the authorities and decisions — what was restored, what was removed and why, and who authorised each change.

The file tells a complete, dated story: this was the condition, this is what we did, this is the evidence it is dry. Build it as the job happens, not afterwards from memory, because records made at the time are accurate and are what an assessor or a court will accept. Each photograph is captioned with what it shows and where; each reading is tied to a labelled point and an instrument; each decision names who approved it. That trail protects the customer, the technician and the insurer alike, and it is the practical expression of working with due care and skill. A good file is also a teaching tool: the next technician can pick up the job, read the plan and the trend, and continue without re-measuring from scratch.

See it

The timeline shows what is captured at each stage, from first attendance to verification.

Do it in metric

Record a monitoring day for the Canberra job. On day 3 you log the drying-zone air at 24 °C and 55 %RH, about 9.9 g/kg, against outside air at about 12 g/kg — the zone is drier, so drying is working. The wet wall points have moved from 28 % to 18 % against a 12 % dry standard, across the 16 m² affected area. Those four figures, dated and tied to labelled points, are a day’s defensible evidence.

Field download

The Defensible job-file checklist lists every record the file must hold, in the order it is captured, with a daily-reading row for °C, %RH and g/kg.

Check yourself

The module check asks what the file must contain, why you build it as you go, and which readings prove drying. Each answer carries a practitioner “why”.

Takeaway

Build the file as the job happens: dated photos, a moisture map, daily metric readings and recorded decisions. It is your proof. Next lesson: the Australian insurance context around that file.

lessons.title: The Australian insurance context
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Legal references are drafted conservatively and flagged for verification.

On the job

A small restoration business in regional Victoria wins steady work from one insurer’s panel. On a kitchen flood the owner asks the technician to “just dry it all and we’ll sort the paperwork later’’, and to promise the cabinets will be “as good as new’’. Both shortcuts are traps: work outside the agreed scope that no one authorised, and a promise the business cannot guarantee. Knowing the Australian insurance and consumer context keeps the job — and the business — out of trouble.

The idea

Most water-damage work in Australia is delivered inside an insurance claim, so the job file is also a claim document, and a few Australian realities shape the work. Scope and authority: work is usually carried out to an agreed scope, and changes — extra drying days, removing a material, engaging another trade — should be authorised and recorded, not assumed. Evidence expectations: insurers and their assessors expect measured drying evidence — readings trending to a dry standard — not “it looks dry”; your metric readings are the proof. Consumer protection: the Australian Consumer Law gives consumers automatic guarantees for services, including that services are provided with due care and skill and are fit for any purpose made known; that is why you avoid over-claiming — do not promise a material is “sterilised” or guarantee a fixed dry time you cannot control. Pricing: quotes and invoices are in Australian dollars (AUD), noting GST where it applies. Disputes: a clear, dated, measured file is your best protection if a claim is questioned months later.

Restoration is a trusted role. You are drying someone’s home or business and creating the record an insurer relies on, often while the occupants are displaced and anxious. Accuracy, honesty and good documentation are the professional standard, and they are also the commercial one: panels keep the contractors whose files are clean and whose promises are realistic. Explain what you can and cannot guarantee in plain English, confirm scope changes before you act on them, and keep the written trail — the same discipline that makes a job defensible also makes a business dependable.

See it

The diagram links the job file to scope, authority, evidence, AUD pricing and consumer guarantees.

Do it in metric

Quote the Victorian job honestly in AUD. Drying equipment that runs on 230 V is costed per day: say 5 days of hire and monitoring at an agreed day rate. Suppose the agreed labour and equipment total is $1200 AUD; GST at 10 % adds $120, for $1320 AUD inc GST. If the readings on day 5 have not reached the 12 % dry standard, you seek authority for extra days in writing rather than quietly extending the job or leaving it wet.

Field download

The Defensible job-file checklist closes with an insurance-context section: scope agreed, changes authorised, pricing in AUD with GST, and no over-claiming.

Check yourself

The module check asks why scope changes are authorised, what evidence insurers expect, and what over-claiming to avoid. Each answer carries a practitioner “why”.

Takeaway

Work to an agreed scope, prove drying with measured evidence, price in AUD with GST, and never over-claim. Next: the module check, then the final knowledge check that closes the course.
